# MASTER CLOSING FRAMEWORK — Grand Slam Sequence
*Ascend Prime Wealth · Drafted 2026-08-10 · Built exclusively from Constantine's Sales Structure doc, the Alan+Constantine Krisp coaching sessions, and real won/lost APW call recordings. Full evidence-cited version lives in Notion (SOP Library → "MASTER CLOSING FRAMEWORK — Grand Slam Sequence"). This copy is Gamma-ready: paste into Gamma → "Paste in text" → presentation.*

**Architecture: Intro/Frame → Discovery → Transition → Pitch → Close.**
Design principle (Constantine, verbatim): Discovery exists to get "the information we need that is relevant to what we will pitch, reveal emotional leverage for the prospect to take action now, build rapport, and **eliminate objections before the close**." The close is not where objections are fought — a properly-run call has already made them impossible. The primary emotion the prospect must feel: **SAFETY**.

---

## PART I — INTRO / FRAME (2–5 min)

**Step 1 — Welcome + Location.** Zero-stakes first contact: "So — where are you calling from?" then relate genuinely. *Pre-handles guardedness: two easy answers put them in answering rhythm.*

**Step 2 — Source + Motivation (harvest self-sold data).** "How did you find us — ad or referral?" → "What motivated you to reach out?" → acknowledge (SELF-SOLD DATA). *Their stated motivation becomes callback ammunition for the pitch and close.*

**Step 3 — Permission-Based "Why Us" (metrics, not credentials).** "Before we start, would it be helpful if I gave you background on the company and the agenda?" → origin story: 500 score → $500K+ personal funding; in business since 2023; $10M+ generated for clients. Close the loop: "Was that context helpful?" Rule: metrics only, no name-dropping. *Pre-handles "are you licensed?" (track record vs paper) and burned-before.*

**Step 4 — Strong Frame: pressure-off agenda + definitive yes/no contract.** THE highest-leverage pre-handle: "The purpose of this call is to walk through our process, see if we're a good fit, and see if we can actually help you. If we can — we discuss details later in the call. If not — we point you in the right direction, no big deal, no hard feelings, we part as friends. All I ask is that by the end, out of respect to both of us, you give me a simple **definitive yes or no**. Sound good?" *Pre-handles "I need to think about it" + rebuilds trust with burned prospects (preceded the $12K Leo signature).*

**Step 5 — Partner Reconfirmation Checkpoint.** "Before we start — is everyone on who'd be needed for financials: PG, treasurer, partners? Just you, or?" (Full partner qualification lives in triage; this is a 10-second reconfirm.) *Kills "I need to talk to my spouse/partner" an hour before it could be said.*

## PART II — DISCOVERY (20–30 min)

**Step 6 — Main Challenge + Business Background.** "If everything was perfect we wouldn't be speaking — what's the main bottleneck?" / "How does your business operate?" Drill with impact questions. Frame first: background questions determine whether funding is even the right path. *They describe their own problem → value objections die.*

**Step 7 — Money Block.** "How much funding?" → "How will you invest it?" → "Why — what changes, specifically?" → "What does funding let you do that you couldn't otherwise — now and future?" Pullback preframe: "Not everyone needs funding… I want to recommend what you actually need." *The fee is later compared against THEIR ROI number, not zero.*

**Step 8 — Runway Stretch.** "Most clients don't budget far enough ahead. We suggest 6–18 months of runway — how much would six months take?" (Real result: $150–200K became "$400K to be comfortable" in 90 seconds.) *They upsize their own goal.*

**Step 9 — Credit Qualification (three-fold rationale).** "Now I'll shift into credit — so we know IF we can fund you, HOW MUCH, and HOW FAST." Scores per bureau, top limit (10K+ preferred / 5K ok / 2.5K minimum), tradelines, age, derogs, utilization, inquiries, business age. Every number on the table before pricing. *Never quote before the full report — prevents post-sale surprises and guarantee disputes.*

**Step 10 — Efforts + How Long (mine their failures).** "Tried getting funding before? With a company or yourself? Why didn't you continue? What were your solo results?" (The $2K same-day close answered: "It was a disaster. No success at all.") *Kills DIY-ego and burned-before at once — the pitch fixes what THEY said failed.*

**Step 11 — Expectation Check (the Ghani question).** "So I set expectations properly — some people expect a licensed broker they hand a package to. What we actually are is coaching/consulting + lender database + done-for-you execution. Which were you picturing?" *Kills the broker-mismatch that once ended a 60-minute call at the close.*

**Step 12 — Bucket Discernment (prospect self-selects).** "Three buckets: 1) teach me, 2) do it for me, 3) hybrid — do it for me while teaching me so I can fund myself forever. Which fits you?" Assumptive variant: "Normally we teach this — but you're super busy, so that doesn't sound like you, correct?" *Kills "I could do this myself." Danger: bucket 1 + expert identity = Expert's Ego → pivot to unsell.*

**Step 13 — Timing, Logistics & Commitment.** "Why now vs later? Anything in the way — projects, vacations? Successful clients tie in 30–60 min/day — realistic for you?" Mindset preframe: "when challenges inevitably happen, we coach you through them." *Timing and logistics objections answered on record 30 minutes early.*

**Step 14 — Prompt for Missed Info.** "Anything else I need to know to make the best recommendation?" *No late-surfacing detonations.*

## PART III — TRANSITION

**Step 15 — Summary → Certainty Statement → Permission to Pitch.** Summarize → "Based on everything you've told me, you fit the profile of our most successful clients. Ready for me to walk you through our process A-Z?" Certainty statement: "I've gone through 100+ competitor offers. They over-promise and under-deliver; their numbers are unrealistic (we state a range); their salespeople have never funded themselves." *Names exactly how they got burned; they invite the pitch (third yes).*

## PART IV — PITCH (5–10 min)

**Step 16 — Preface.** "The goal: $___ in funding. How we've done it — 500→$500K personally, $10M+ for clients — is a three-stage process." Slides: 1–2 per stage, bullets only; closer does the talking.

**Step 17 — Stage 1: Credit Optimization.** Callback→Solution→Benefit→Prompt. Callback THEIR numbers → cleanup, inquiry removal, utilization 1–7% → "OPTIMIZED FOR FUNDING — AUTOMATED HIGH-LIMIT APPROVALS." Winning frame: "we bring the banks your report on a silver platter — every reason to say yes, no reason to say no." → "What questions on that specifically?"

**Step 18 — Stage 2: Funding Strategy & Approvals.** "Your customized funding sequence — specific to your geolocation and profile: where we go, what we say, what we do" (12,000+ data-point institution database). Prompt again. *The strategy layer is the moat DIY can't replicate.*

**Step 19 — Stage 3: Execution & Advanced Strategies.** "The stage everyone loves — approvals, compounding to your $___ goal and beyond." Wrap with the full-arc question across all three stages.

**Step 20 — Temp Check 1–10 (the keystone self-sell).** "How are you feeling about the whole process, 1–10?" 8+ → "What would be especially beneficial?" Below 8 → "What would make you a 10?" **They must sell themselves out loud.** Discipline: an evasive answer means certainty is NOT built — loop back; never proceed to price. An uncured "7" becomes "I'll do research."

**Step 21 — Next Steps / Future Pace.** 10–15 seconds: "Agreement → payment → onboarding: easy videos, day-by-day." *Yes now has a picture.*

**Step 22 — Investment: Grand Slam Offer Assembly.** Order: **VALUE STACK → ROI → PRICE DROP → SILENCE.** Five components:
1. **Refundable deposit + funding guarantee** — "$2,000 upfront, refundable if $20K minimum isn't secured — a 10x return. Make sense?" (current calibration: $5K / $50K floor)
2. **Best case / worst case** — "Best: significant funding, the fee becomes irrelevant. Worst: full refund PLUS a written explanation of why. Either way you win."
3. **Transparency stack** — walk the whole tiered fee table aloud (6% first $100K → 1% above $1M; milestone-keyed success fees; "under $40K funded you pay nothing") — "and it's all in writing." Minor cons first, then pro-stack.
4. **Ask for MORE — never preemptively discount.** The $15K close came from asking higher. Ladder $8K→$6K→$4K→$2K exists only for live objections, backend rising as upfront falls.
5. **Micro-commitment floor** — $300 deposit keeps a money-tight deal alive.
Then: **silence.**

## PART V — CLOSE

**Step 23 — Answer All + Assume the Sale.** "Ready to get started, or any questions?" → "Ready to get the ball rolling?" (never "Is anything stopping you?"). If Steps 1–22 ran, this is administrative.

**Step 24 — Objections: Isolate + Solve (4-category diagnostic: Uncertainty / Finances / Partner / Timing).** The elimination walk: "Makes sense? You understand it? You want the funding? Time's committed, partner's on board… so the only piece left is the fee itself." Call out the unspoken: "Prospects never say 'it's not worth it' to your face — 0% of the time — but they think it. Do you have the finances, and do you see the value?" "Think about it" → "Walk me through your thought process." Same answer twice → suggest the objection yourself and re-open that stage. Guarantee questions: "I can't control any institution's protocols. What I can say: we make your profile so underwriting-green-light compatible that it becomes very, very unreasonable not to succeed." **Every objection maps backward: Uncertainty→16–20 · Finances→7+22 · Partner→5 · Timing→13. An objection = a skipped step. Fix the step, not the symptom.**

**Step 25 — Safety, Personal Guarantee, Agreement LAST.** "My reputation is on the line. I only deserve your money if I deliver value." Guarantee = personal integrity, not a clause. Agreement presented last, after everything is resolved. (This exact cycle closed the $12K.)

**Step 26 — Pull-Back + Booked Next Step (never a dead end).** "The decision is yours — ball's in your court." Analytical stallers: project certainty, book a concrete 20-min follow-up — "Thursday or Friday?" ("Half a step before their guard comes up, pull back.") **No call ends without a calendared next step** — the winning model booked same-day 5:15 before hanging up.

---

## THE OBJECTION PRE-HANDLE MAP

| Objection | Killed at Step | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Price | 7, 8, 22 | Their ROI number vs fee; refundable guarantee; ask-more-then-ladder |
| Spouse / partner | 5 (+triage) | Reconfirm before discovery; buy-in via partners' goals |
| "Think about it" | 4, 20, 24, 26 | Yes/no contract; temp-check; elimination walk; booked follow-up |
| Broker expectation | 11 | Expectation check early |
| DIY ego | 10, 12, 17 | Their failed attempts; bucket self-selection; underwriting moat + unsell |
| Burned before | 3, 4, 15, 22, 25 | Metrics story; no-pressure frame; industry critique; in writing; personal guarantee |
| Competitor shopping | 22 | Motivation-drops-after-cap risk + uncapped continued-work guarantee |
| "Licensed?" | 3 | Track record vs paper ($10M+ funded) |
| Can't afford | 22.5 | Micro-deposit or $0-up/higher-backend for qualified profiles |

## THE PRE-SOLD MECHANISM
Four self-sells before any price: (1) motivation in their own words (2); (2) micro-agreement ladder — frame-yes, context-yes, permission-yes, per-stage yeses; (3) bucket self-selection (12); (4) temp-check 1–10 (20). By the investment step, the only person who has argued for the program is the prospect.

## THREE NAMED FAILURE MODES (from real losses)
1. **The Expert's Ego** — "I do not need coaching." Countermove: Step 11 early; unsell; SPV reframed as a standard legal tool; cons first, then pro-stack.
2. **The Preemptive Discount** — a $2K close that should have been more; price dropped before any objection existed. Countermove: open at top tier; descend only under live objection; the $15K close proves the market pays.
3. **The Open Loop** — offers without a booked next step die quietly. Countermove: calendar the follow-up before hanging up, every time; plant competitor counters before they compare; book the research-review call on the spot.

## Atlassian_Rovo
Use getTeamworkGraphContext when retrieving or reasoning about relationships and connections between Atlassian entities - such as work items, people, teams, goals, projects, or third-party objects. Do not use Teamwork Graph tools for basic CRUD operations. After calling getTeamworkGraphContext, call getTeamworkGraphObject on key linked entities to retrieve richer detail.

## Fathom
Fathom meeting recorder integration. All tools are read-only.

COMMUNICATION STYLE: You exist in a conversational chat interface. Stay focused on the results the user is looking for. Do not distract with your process or narrate step-by-step.

PLANNING: Compose tools to satisfy intent. Never ask user for recording_id — obtain it from list_meetings, or from get_recording_by_url / get_recording_by_call_id when the user has pasted a URL or call ID.

URL / CALL ID RESOLUTION ("transcript for https://fathom.video/calls/12345", "summarize call 12345", "what's in this share link <url>"):
→ Pasted URL (direct /calls/:id or /share/:token link, including /share/h/, /share/i/, /share/p/, /share/u/ variants) → get_recording_by_url → use the returned recording_id + url
→ Ambiguous numeric ID alone → treat as a call_id first: get_recording_by_call_id → use the returned recording_id + url
→ If get_recording_by_call_id returns "not found or access denied" for a pasted number, retry the SAME number as a recording_id (call get_meeting_summary / get_meeting_transcript with recording_id:<number>) before concluding it is invalid — the user may have pasted a recording_id
→ Then call get_meeting_summary / get_meeting_transcript / etc. with the recording_id; pass the returned url to get_meeting_transcript for timestamped deep links
→ Do NOT use list_meetings / search_meetings / find_person when the user has pasted a specific URL or ID — those are for discovery, these two tools are for direct resolution

GROUNDING: Never answer questions about what was said, decided, or described in a meeting without first calling tools. Do not infer or summarize meeting content from memory. Any factual claim about "what X said" or "what the symptoms were" must come from a get_meeting_transcript call. If no tools have been called yet for a content question, call them first — then answer.

IDENTITY: get_identity returns the authenticated user's name and email. Call it once per session when you need to identify the user. Do not automatically apply the retur… [truncated]

## Figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

## Gamma
Gamma creates AI-powered presentations, documents, webpages, and social posts. Only include optional parameters when the user explicitly requests or clearly implies them. Gamma has intelligent defaults - when in doubt, omit. When uncertain about user preferences, ask rather than assume. The read_gamma tool can read the content of an existing Gamma when given its file ID. Existing gammas have a type: "template" or "regular". Only templates can be used with generate_from_template; use get_gammas with type="template" to discover valid templates. Non-template IDs are not valid inputs to generate_from_template. If generate_from_template reports that an ID is inaccessible or not a template, find a valid template with get_gammas(type="template"). If the user's intent is to create a new gamma, but not by using an existing template, then use the generate tool. IMPORTANT: The tools provided by this server cannot edit or modify existing gammas. Do not suggest that you can make changes, adjustments, or refinements to a generated gamma. Instead, let the user know they can customize their gamma directly in the Gamma editor.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

## Krisp
This server provides access to the authenticated user's Krisp workspace data including meetings, transcripts, action items, and calendar. The user's timezone and display preferences are available as part of the workspace context.

## Nimble
Nimble turns the web into structured data. Use these product names exactly: Search, Answer, Extract, Extraction Template, Web Search Agent, Map, Crawl. Never call an Extraction Template a Web Search Agent (or vice versa).

Route by intent:

1. Named site + a direct item (URL or site-specific ID): nimble_extract_templates_list → get → run. Prefer a Nimble-maintained Extraction Template. If none matches, use a Web Search Agent — do not generate a new Extraction Template and do not dump a raw Extract.

2. Web Search Agent (nimble_agents_*): research, data enrichment, dataset building, named-subject information gathering, "extract all …" without a URL, catalog/directory entity lists, and any fan-out beyond 1–few already-known URLs. Reuse order: nimble_agents_list → nimble_agent_templates_list → create/run. Classify use_case before create/run: research = open-ended gathering/synthesis (named-subject dossiers, briefings, site/product deep dives); dataset_building = entity lists/tables by criteria or geo, catalogs, "extract all …" without a URL; enrichment = add fields to records the user already has (list, CSV, named items) via web lookup. Set effort from the task — do not ask the user to pick: low/medium for fast simple asks; high as the default once several fields need real digging; x-high/max for complex multi-faceted profiles (financials, filings, history). dataset_building requires high or above. For a quick first look, offer a preview at low then re-run at the recommended tier. Poll nimble_agents_run_status then nimble_agents_run_result. Gallery templates (nimble_agent_templates_*) are not Extraction Templates.

3. Search (nimble_search): only a single closed lookup — who/what at a glance, filing/page pointer, reverse lookup, named-channel presence. For a closed synthesized fact, set include_answer=true (Answer). Do not complete research or dataset asks with Search.

4. Extract (nimble_extract): one known URL, one-time. Check Extraction Templates first when the site is named. Not for "extract all", catalogs, or m… [truncated]

## Trello
You are connected to the Trello MCP server. To identify the current user, call the `trelloReadMember` tool with `action: "get_me"` — it returns the authenticated user's Trello profile.

Dates & times: all date-time fields are UTC ISO 8601 (e.g. "2026-06-01T17:00:00.000Z"). This covers `due` on trelloWriteCard and trelloWriteInbox (card due dates), and `start`/`end` on trelloWritePlanner (calendar events). For local or relative times (e.g. "Friday 5pm"), convert to UTC using the user's timezone: for cards and Inbox, call trelloReadMember ("get_me") for `prefs.timezone`; for planner events, call trelloReadPlanner ("get") for `primaryCalendar.timezone`. When a date is given with no time, default to 09:00 in the user's local timezone.

Inbox: the Inbox is a personal quick-capture surface, not a normal board. To view or manage it, use trelloReadInbox and trelloWriteInbox — do not use trelloReadBoard to list or find Inbox cards.

Ordered creation: when creating multiple lists or cards that must keep a specific order, set `pos` to sequential integers (1, 2, 3, …) in the intended order — per list for cards, and across the board for lists. Each position is a distinct value, so lists and cards can be created in parallel without their positions colliding.

properties.Verification: A decision is recorded here with a date, and either (a) both are confirmed retained with the retention gap addressed by a written SOP + checklist they work from, or (b) offboarding is executed and their open files - Matt L.'s Experian/BofA reinsertion (Grace) and Ed C.'s TransUnion dispute (Anne) - are formally reassigned with no dropped items.
properties.Evidence / Links: Raised 8/27. Alan is considering TERMINATING the dispute team over a specific, repeated failure: Anne and Grace are NOT RETAINING INFORMATION between sessions - the same instructions have to be re-given. He is trialing them through this week before deciding. \|\| WHY THIS IS A REAL RISK, NOT A STAFFING GRIPE: they hold live client work right now. Grace owns the Bank of America reinsertion / 605B packet on Matt L.; Anne owns Ed C.'s TransUnion dispute. Both files are already time-sensitive (Ed's expedited 7-day dispute window opened 8/27; Matt's Experian thread is stalled and needs a fresh filing). A termination without a reassignment plan drops both. \|\| DIAGNOSTIC WORTH RUNNING FIRST: the retention failure started before there was a written dispute SOP or the Trello board (both introduced 8/25). It is genuinely unclear whether this is a people problem or a systems problem - if there was nothing durable to retain FROM, retention was never going to happen. That distinction should inform the decision, and it is cheap to test: give one week working strictly from the Trello board + written checklist, and see whether the repeats stop. \|\| NEEDED FROM ALAN: the ruling, and if it is termination, who picks up the two live files.

properties.Item: New daily meeting cadence set (7:00 Daily Sync / 7:30 Daily Ops / 8:15 Dispute Team) - confirm it holds and is on calendars
properties.Verification: All three meetings exist as recurring calendar invites with the right attendees, and one full week runs without a skipped session. Fathom/recording confirmed attached to at least the Ops and Dispute Team calls so decisions land in the record rather than only in the room.
properties.Evidence / Links: Established 8/27. Three standing daily meetings: 7:00 AM DAILY SYNC, 7:30 AM DAILY OPS, 8:15 AM DISPUTE TEAM. \|\| WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND SCHEDULING: this is a direct answer to the new-hire complaint about 'structure and disorganization' that started this whole build-out - a fixed daily rhythm is the single cheapest structural fix available. It also gives the dispute team the recurring checkpoint that its retention problem needs (see the Anne & Grace decision row). \|\| RISK TO WATCH: cadence set in a conversation is not cadence that survives a busy week. The verification standard is one clean week, not the announcement.

properties.Item: OUTREACH: Lynn to lead an Instagram DM setting campaign (ManyChat / Mochi under evaluation)
properties.Verification: A tool is chosen with the reason recorded; the DM funnel writes into GHL with source/campaign tags so DM-sourced leads are attributable in the Ad Scoreboard rather than landing as 'Source: Unknown'; and the first booked call traced end-to-end from DM to calendar.
properties.Evidence / Links: Assigned 8/27 - Lynn's role expands from her prior scope to LEADING an Instagram DM setting campaign. Tooling under research: MANYCHAT and MOCHI. \|\| THIS IS A NEW ACQUISITION CHANNEL, and it arrives with the same trap the Meta ads had: the tracking has to be built BEFORE volume, not after. Every lead currently in the tracker sourced outside the Meta form reads 'Attribution Confidence: Missing' - and the two leads added today (Robert M., Chris M.) are both examples, with no source or booking channel captured at all. If DM leads flow in untagged, the Ad Scoreboard silently understates or misattributes performance and the channel cannot be judged. \|\| PREREQUISITE: whichever tool is picked must hand off into GHL with a distinct source value and campaign tag. That is a five-minute configuration on day one and an unrecoverable data gap if skipped.

properties.Evidence / Links: Scoped 8/28 ([fathom.video/calls/801234866](http://fathom.video/calls/801234866)) - build a real-time dashboard in Claude Code pulling from GoHighLevel and Meta Ads to identify and fix funnel bottlenecks. Jacob Rosales to send Alan the dashboard prompt along with the ad scripts, handoff skill, Meta Ads SOP and checklist. \|\| THIS IS THE PROPER FIX FOR WHAT THE DAILY SWEEPS HAVE BEEN APPROXIMATING. The Notion tracker reconstructs the funnel from call recordings after the fact; a live GHL+Meta pull would show it as it happens, and would close the attribution gap that leaves most non-Meta-form leads reading 'Attribution Confidence: Missing'. \|\| BLOCKED THE SAME WAY EVERYTHING GHL IS BLOCKED: GHL uses header auth and the PIT is local-only, so this must be built from Claude Code on Alan's PC, not from a cloud session. The runbook for the local pull is already written (LOCAL_PULL_RUNBOOK, Drive id 1RqEpBa4Em1iwE_GdHhuk_kxhotBYXPjx). \|\| DEPENDENCY WORTH SEQUENCING: build it AFTER the Meta URL parameters and GHL source tags are set, not before. A dashboard over untagged traffic reports the same 'unknown' the tracker already does.

properties.Item: 4-DAY DISPUTE DOCTRINE captured - Ina to write a personal SOP + Loom; accepting a 30-day investigation is a process failure
properties.Verification: Ina's SOP and Loom are submitted and filed in the SOP Library; the 'Dispute Team Updates' doc exists and is shared with Ina + Ashwini; and the next 4-day attempt shows the supervisor ask actually made, on a recorded call.
properties.Evidence / Links: From the 8/27 dispute-process call ([fathom.video/calls/801867207](http://fathom.video/calls/801867207)) and the 8/28 ops call ([fathom.video/calls/802994217](http://fathom.video/calls/802994217)). Alan to create and share a 'Dispute Team Updates' doc with Ina + Ashwini; Ina then builds the SOP/Loom and submits it. \|\| THREE DOCTRINE POINTS WORTH PRESERVING VERBATIM - these are the most reusable things said all week: \|\| (1) THE 4-DAY AND 30-DAY TRACKS ARE DIFFERENT ANIMALS. The 4-day process is a separate, LEGALLY MANDATED track for identity theft. AGREEING TO A 30-DAY INVESTIGATION IS ITSELF A PROCESS FAILURE that nearly guarantees a negative outcome. The bureau will offer the 30-day path; taking it is the mistake. This explains outcomes already on the book - Ashwini's 4-day block was denied and she was pushed to a 30-day ending ~Sep 2, and Ed C. was forced to a 30-day on 8/12. \|\| (2) 'VALID' IS NOT AN ANSWER. A bureau claiming an account is valid - e.g. because payments were recently made - is INSUFFICIENT. If the account is inaccurate or not the client's, it must be removed regardless of payment activity. \|\| (3) ASK FOR A SUPERVISOR. The concrete failure that prompted the SOP was this step being skipped on the Brenda call. Inconsistent 4-day outcomes traced to missed steps, not to bad luck. \|\| PLUS A FOURTH, FROM THE 8/28 CALL - THE FTC ALLOWANCE TACTIC: when new negatives surface, argue they are part of a SINGLE ONGOING IDENTITY THEFT EVENT rather than filing a fresh FTC report per item, because the client's FTC report allowance is limited and burning one per item exhausts it. \|\| ⭐ THIS IS THE ANSWER TO THE 'SOP LIBRARY IS JUNK' COMPLAINT. It is specific, it is operational, it names the failure mode and the countermove, and it came from a real call rather than from a summary of a summary. Write the library entries this way.

properties.Item: ICP MISMATCH - fix SCIO ad campaign targeting; current leads require excessive effort for low-ticket sales and carry legal risk
properties.Verification: SCIO targeting is revised and the next two weeks of leads are measured against the new 3-5 cards / \$10K+ limit / 2+ yr age standard. Success is the share of booked calls meeting it rising, not raw lead volume.
properties.Evidence / Links: Named 8/28 as the IMMEDIATE PRIORITY ([fathom.video/calls/803053542](http://fathom.video/calls/803053542)): current leads are not the Ideal Customer Profile, they require excessive effort for low-ticket sales, and they create LEGAL RISK. \|\| THE WORKED EXAMPLE IS MICHAEL MOORE: near bankruptcy, no income, in a debt-relief program, and the only strategy that fit his file was a gray-area one that he himself refused. A funnel that delivers that profile to a closer is not a closing problem, it is a targeting problem - and the legal exposure is created upstream of anyone's script. \|\| SUPPORTING NUMBER: only 1-3 prospects qualified for the primary offer in all of August. \|\| CONNECTED WORK, SAME ROOT CAUSE - keep these four together or they will be fixed separately and half-shipped: SCIO targeting (this row), the numeric qualification standard, the DM triage script with the 30-day timeline question first, and the OPM video creatives. \|\| STRATEGIC FRAME SET THE SAME DAY ([fathom.video/calls/802994217](http://fathom.video/calls/802994217)) - 'TOP OF MARKET FIT': optimize all messaging and process for the ideal client (high credit, high income) on the theory that doing so attracts them directly and still naturally captures the broader market below. Alan to film a Loom on it. That is the principle this targeting fix is meant to express.

Also established a Trello convention: tasks with unclear solutions move to a 'Do Not Know/Understand' list so the 'Priority' list stays trustworthy. || Pricing note: the $100/hr is the FIFTH distinct pricing structure in circulation.

properties.Title: Dispute process: refining the 4-day track
properties.Outcome: Ina mandated to write a personal SOP for the 4-day dispute process. Core doctrine captured.
properties.Summary: THE MOST SOP-DENSE CALL OF THE WEEK. (Experian answering a canceled dispute)"}, "content": "> **Status: drafted from two real calls, not yet approved by Alan.** Ina is writing her own personal version of this as a checklist + Loom. This page is the shared reference the personal SOPs should agree with.

## Why this SOP exists

4-day dispute outcomes have been **inconsistent** — and the diagnosis on the 8/27 call was blunt: the failures trace to **missed steps, not bad luck**. Every point below is a step someone skipped on a real call.

---

## Rule 1 — The 4-day and 30-day tracks are different animals

The 4-day process is a **separate, legally mandated track for identity theft**. It is not a faster version of the standard dispute.

**Agreeing to a 30-day investigation is itself a process failure.** It nearly guarantees a negative outcome. The bureau representative will offer the 30-day path — often helpfully, as though it is the same thing. Taking it is the mistake.

input.content:
> **Drafted from two real calls, not yet approved by Alan.** Ina is writing her own personal checklist + Loom version. This page is the shared reference those should agree with.

## Why this SOP exists

4-day dispute outcomes have been **inconsistent**, and the 8/27 diagnosis was blunt: the failures trace to **missed steps, not bad luck**. Every rule below is a step someone actually skipped on a real call.

---

## Rule 1 — The 4-day and 30-day tracks are different animals

The 4-day process is a **separate, legally mandated track for identity theft**. It is not a faster version of the standard dispute.

**Agreeing to a 30-day investigation is itself a process failure.** It nearly guarantees a negative outcome. The bureau rep will offer the 30-day path, often helpfully, as though it is the same thing. Taking it is the mistake.

What this has already cost, on live files:

| Client | What happened | Where it lands |
|---|---|---|
| Ashwini A. | 4-day fraud block **denied**, pushed to 30-day | ~Sep 2 |
| Ed C. | 605B block refused on two Hancock Whitney accounts, **forced 30-day** opened 8/12 | ~Sep 11 |

Two of the highest-priority files on the book are sitting in the slow lane. That is what this rule being unwritten has cost.

---

## Rule 2 — "Valid" is not an answer

A bureau claiming an account is **valid** — typically because payments were recently made on it — is **insufficient**.

Recent payment activity says nothing about whether the account belongs to the client. If the account is **inaccurate or not the client's, it must be removed**, regardless of payment history. Do not accept validity as a closing argument and do not let the call end there.

---

## Rule 3 — Ask for a supervisor

The specific failure that prompted this SOP: the supervisor ask was **skipped on the Brenda call**.

Ask every time. The frontline rep is working from a script that treats the 4-day track as an exception; the supervisor is the level where the statutory obligation is actually recognized.

---

## Rule 4 — One identity-theft event, not one FTC report per item

When **new** negative items surface mid-engagement, argue that they are part of a **single ongoing identity theft event** rather than filing a fresh FTC report for each item.

The reason is concrete and not rhetorical: **a client's FTC report allowance is limited.** Burning one per item exhausts it, and then the remedy is gone when it is most needed. Frame late-arriving items as further manifestations of the event already reported.

---

## Escalation path — when general support keeps failing

Two escalation levers, both proven on this book:

1. **Experian Special Handling** — not general support. Assigned 8/28 for Ed C. (address corrections), and for Ashwini + Matthew.
2. **Cite CFPB documentation** on the call as leverage.

**Record the call and send it to Alan.** This is mandatory, not optional. Recording is what produced the documented non-compliance pattern on Matt L.'s TransUnion file, where the bureau cited "internal criteria" while refusing to give a specific decline reason. The bureau's exact refusal language is the asset.

---

## Failure mode worth naming: the bureau answering the wrong dispute

On Matt L. (8/27), Experian's responses were referencing an **old dispute canceled on Aug 5** — not the live reinsertion/605B filing. Nothing on the current workstream was being adjudicated at all.

If a file shows no movement, check that the bureau is responding to the dispute you think it is before assuming the argument is losing. The remedy is to **stop chasing the existing thread and file fresh with correct, current documentation**.

---

## Checklist — run this on every 4-day attempt

- [ ] Confirmed this is the 4-day identity-theft track, and said so on the call
- [ ] **Declined** any offer to convert it to a 30-day investigation
- [ ] Did not accept "valid" / "recent payments" as a reason to keep an account
- [ ] **Asked for a supervisor**
- [ ] Framed any new items as the same ongoing event, not a new FTC report
- [ ] Escalated to Special Handling if general support stalled
- [ ] Cited CFPB documentation where applicable
- [ ] **Recorded the call and sent it to Alan**
- [ ] Logged status to the `dispute team agenda` Slack channel and the Trello board
- [ ] Confirmed the bureau is responding to the *current* filing, not a superseded one

> **Drafted 8/28 from the Robert Morawitz call and the DM triage revision. Needs Alan's sign-off before it becomes binding on setters.**

## The problem this solves

In all of August, **only 1–3 prospects qualified for the primary offer.** Closers spent full hours on files that could never fund. The 8/28 diagnosis named it as an **ICP mismatch** — a targeting problem, not a closing problem — and noted it also creates **legal risk**, because the only strategies that fit an unfundable profile tend to be gray-area ones.

Until now every qualification rule was a judgment call: "squinty-eyed leads," "high utilization with a low ask." Those require credit training to apply. The three numbers below do not.

---

## The filter — three numbers, askable in a DM

A prospect should clear **all three** before a full funding call is booked:

| # | Criterion | Why it matters to underwriting |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **3–5 credit cards** | Fewer than three reads as a thin, unbuilt file. There is no history to underwrite. |
| 2 | **At least one card with a $10K+ limit** | Existing high limits are what other lenders use to justify high limits. A file topping out at $500 signals that no one has yet extended real trust. |
| 3 | **2+ year average account age** | Age is the input that cannot be manufactured quickly. It is the difference between a fixable file and a long project. |

---

## The case that forced it

**Robert Morawitz, 8/27** ([fathom.video/calls/798787726](http://fathom.video/calls/798787726)) booked and consumed an entire funding call while holding:

- Two revolving cards, limits **$300 and $500**
- Income **under $50K**
- Scores 693–698
- Asking for **$1M+** for real estate fix-and-flips

He failed all three criteria. The call ended in disqualification and a $100/hr consulting downsell. **All three filters would have caught him in a two-minute DM exchange.**

---

## Ship it together with the timeline question

The DM triage revision moves **"when do you want to start"** to the **top** of the script, with a firm **30-day funding timeline** as the filter. That question and these three numbers are both pre-call filters and they belong in the same script revision — shipping them separately means half of it gets done.

Full DM triage set: funding amount · **timeline ≤ 30 days** · prior attempts · how they will deploy the money · industry · ~700+ score · **the three card criteria above**.

---

## What to do with a prospect who fails

Failing is not the same as worthless. The honest paths:

- **Nurture / profile-building** — the path Michael M. and Stefan are on. Set a real follow-up date, do not leave it open.
- **Consulting downsell** — currently quoted at $100/hr, but ⚠️ **this is unratified**. It is the fifth pricing structure in circulation and Alan has not ruled on whether hourly consulting is an approved product. Do not quote it as settled.

**Never** reach for a strategy that only works because the profile is unfundable. That is the ICP mismatch turning into legal exposure, and on 8/27 it was the *client* who caught it rather than us.

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content - tables, code, diagrams - gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-0/bundled-skills/2.1.251/8bbfd6c8353d313b0558f3ec181ab61a/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

# Artifact runtime capabilities

A published Artifact page can declare **runtime capabilities** — abilities the claude.ai viewer grants the page at open time — by passing `capabilities: {name: config}` to the Artifact tool. The control plane is the authority on valid names and config shapes. Declaration gestures: **omitting** `capabilities` on a redeploy carries the stored declaration forward unchanged (and preserves the artifact's stored contract pin); an **empty object** `{}` is the explicit clear-all; a **non-empty object** is a full-set declaration (anything stored but not restated is revoked). Moving a republished artifact's runtime version is a deliberate gesture — pass `contract: 'latest'` to upgrade, or a specific version to pin or roll back — never a side effect of editing.

**Available capabilities:** `artifact`, `db`, `downloads`, `mcp`, `room`, `sample`, `self` — the complete set of capability names you may declare. Anything not listed is unavailable to this user.

Runtime contract 0.2.31


Capability namespaces live behind `claude.use(name)`: `const db = await claude.use("db")` resolves the capability's namespace, or `null` when this view cannot run it (not served, not granted, or failed to load — indistinguishable by design). Branch on `null` and design for absence. `window.claude` carries only `use`: no `window.claude.db`, `.room`, or `.artifact` member is ever promised, so never read one — render the page without them and light features up when the promise resolves (later, never within your script's first run, and unordered with DOMContentLoaded; `null` after 10 s when no viewer answers). The resolved namespace is frozen and platform-owned: call its functions and keep the reference; never assign to it, `defineProperty` on it, or replace a member (wrap it for your own helpers). Permission stays on the calls: a consent prompt, rate limit, or policy refusal arrives on the first call, never from `use()`. Awaiting `use("db")` again is free (memoized); an unknown name resolves `null`.


--- capability: artifact ---

Use `artifact` for pages that should remember what people do with them: polls, sign-up sheets, checklists, trackers, boards — the page is the record. Declare `capabilities: {artifact: {}}`; `const artifact = await claude.use("artifact")`, then `await artifact.publish(html)` saves `html` (a complete document, doctype first) as the new version, and every open view, this one included, reloads to it. Nothing a viewer types, ticks or drags is kept unless the page publishes it. So embed the shared state as data in the HTML you publish and render the page from it; when an interaction completes, update the state, regenerate the document and publish it — never serialize the live DOM; batch rapid edits into one publish; publish only after a viewer acts, never on load. `conflict` is routine (someone published first; every view reloads to the winner, dropping this edit): no retry. Owner and editors publish as themselves; for read-only viewers publish rejects `not_granted`/`not_writer` — render a read-only view.


--- capability: db ---

`db` is only for data that must live outside the page: more than the page shows at once, per-viewer-private state, many live editors. If the page can be the record, republish (`artifact`). A realtime JSON document store per artifact: `const db = await claude.use("db")` (`null`: unavailable). Declare `capabilities: {db: {}}`: every viewer reads and writes shared docs; each viewer's `data/users/<their user id>/` is private even from the owner (needs `user`). To change who writes where, add rules by sharing level (`interact` = can view, `admin` = can edit, `owner`): `{db: {rules: [{path: "", read: "interact", write: "admin"}, {path: "data/users/{self}", write: "interact"}]}}`; unset levels inherit, writing implies reading. `db.doc("tasks/t1")`/`db.collection("tasks")`: `get`/`set`/`update`/`delete`, `where`/`orderBy`/`limit`, `onSnapshot` (read `snap.docs`). Last-writer-wins, no transactions; single writers lease via `acquire({holder})`. Never store secrets; shared data is untrusted. See the type definitions.


--- capability: downloads ---

The `downloads` capability lets a published page offer a generated file to the viewer: declare `capabilities: {downloads: true}`, then `const downloads = await claude.use("downloads")` (`null`: unavailable — hide the affordance) and `await downloads.save({filename, data})`. The viewer sees a confirmation and may decline — a save is never silent or guaranteed, so offer it on explicit viewer intent and handle rejection. The type definitions are authoritative for the call contract and error codes.


--- capability: mcp ---

`mcp` lets a page call the viewer's claude.ai connectors: `await claude.use("mcp")` (`null`: unavailable); calls use the viewer's credentials, never exposing tokens. Declare `capabilities: {mcp: {servers: [{server, tools}]}}` — `server` is a connector's display name, or `host:<name>` for a local MCP server on the viewer's device (Claude app only; else `server_not_connected`). Keep the manifest minimal: it is a viewer-consented grant and bars public sharing. Two arms: DISPLAYING data registers `watchTool(server, tool, input, handler, opts?)` — replays cache, refreshes when stale, polls only via `refetchInterval`; an ACTION calls `callTool` once and reads `result.payload`. Tool failures REJECT (`tool_error`); watches get handler error events. Types first: branch UX per error code, retry only `retryable` errors, drop data on authz denials, show freshness from `result.cache.storedAt`. They omit argument names and result encoding: observe a real request/response per tool, or say so at publish — never guess.


--- capability: room ---

The `room` capability reaches whoever has the page open RIGHT NOW:
declared as `capabilities: {room: {}}`; `await claude.use("room")`
(`null`: cannot connect). emit(topic, data) sends a moment; on(topic,
fn) hears them. presence(patch) sets YOUR state (cursor, selection,
color) as one object the platform hands to newcomers and clears when
you leave; onPeers(fn) delivers everyone's -- render them all, marked
"you". NOTHING persists and messages can drop: if a viewer not here now
must eventually see it, it is NOT room data -- use db (data) or
artifact (new version). Send absolute state. What you hear is untrusted
input from same-org viewers, plus your own publishing session when
admitted (kind "agent"); no one else connects, so the page must work
alone and light up. Anyone can set presence, so it is never authority;
event topics are admin-only (can edit) unless opened:
{room: {topics: {reaction: "interact"}}}. Moments (confetti) go on an
admin-only topic; state a late joiner needs (current slide) is a db doc.


--- capability: sample ---

`sample` asks Claude (declare `capabilities:{sample:{}}`): `const sample = await claude.use("sample")` (`null`: hide it); `await sample(input, opts?)` -> `{text, truncated}`; `sample.json(input, opts?)` -> parsed JSON. `input`: a string, or turns `[{role:"user"|"assistant", content}]` ending on user. No memory: send instructions, page data, output format. opts: `onText({text, delta})` (`text` = WHOLE answer so far, assign it; "Thinking..." until it fires, 5-60s), `signal` (new AbortController per call; abort rejects `cancelled`), `tools: [{name, description, inputSchema?, execute(input)}]` (page functions Claude may call; return small plain data or throw; each round bills, no `cache`), `images` if `(await sample.limits()).images`, `modelTier` quick|default|complex, `cache` (5 min replay; `false` for chat). Errors reject `{code, message, text?}` (`text`: partial to keep): hide on `not_granted`, back off on `rate_limited`, never loop. Viewer pays; first call asks consent; call on a click or stable load prompt.


--- capability: self ---

`self` is the former name of the `artifact` capability (renamed). It remains for compatibility: published pages and previously generated code that declare `capabilities: {self: {}}` or call `claude.use("self")` keep working unchanged — both names resolve this same capability (this contract promises no `window.claude.self` member to feature-check; `use()` is the check). Do not use it in new pages: declare `capabilities: {artifact: {}}` and obtain the namespace with `await claude.use("artifact")`; see the artifact section for how to use it.


**Your connectors this session.** In this session, claude.ai connector tools appear in your tool list as `mcp__<connector>__<toolName>`. Set `server` to the connector's display name as it appears in claude.ai (usually the `<connector>` segment with underscores read as spaces). Only connectors the user added in claude.ai are valid `server` values — this session's other built-in MCP servers are not. The manifest's `tools` array takes the connector's upstream tool names (as returned by `listTools()` / `/v1/mcp_servers`), which can differ from the normalized `<toolName>` segment when an upstream name contains `.` or spaces. Every `servers[]` entry needs a non-empty `tools` array naming the tools the page calls — an empty or omitted `tools` list is refused and never means "all tools"; to publish without connector access, leave `mcp` out of `capabilities` (pass `capabilities: {}` to clear a stored declaration) rather than declaring an empty `servers` list. In hermetic/CI sessions where connectors aren't loaded but `$CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` is set, fetch the list via Bash: `curl -H 'anthropic-version: 2023-06-01' -H 'anthropic-beta: mcp-servers-2025-12-04' -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN" https://api.anthropic.com/v1/mcp_servers?limit=1000`; in that case use each entry's `display_name` as the `server` value (exact display names are always accepted alongside tool-prefix segments).

**Call contract** (runtime contract 0.2.31). The platform-served `window.claude` type definitions for this contract are extracted under `/tmp/claude-0/bundled-skills/2.1.251/793a45abe1b12323082059d557da9f44/artifact-capabilities`: `0.2.31/artifact.d.ts`, `0.2.31/claude.d.ts`, `0.2.31/db.d.ts`, `0.2.31/downloads.d.ts`, `0.2.31/mcp.d.ts`, `0.2.31/room.d.ts`, `0.2.31/sample.d.ts`, `0.2.31/self.d.ts`. Read `/tmp/claude-0/bundled-skills/2.1.251/793a45abe1b12323082059d557da9f44/artifact-capabilities/0.2.31/claude.d.ts` (how a page reaches any capability on this contract) and `/tmp/claude-0/bundled-skills/2.1.251/793a45abe1b12323082059d557da9f44/artifact-capabilities/0.2.31/mcp.d.ts` before writing any code that calls the `mcp` capability — they are authoritative for this contract version over any remembered API shape. The type definitions cover only the call envelope — they do not tell you a connector tool's argument names or its result encoding. Never publish a page that calls a connector tool without having observed one real request/response pair for that tool in this session; if you cannot safely observe one (for example, the connector is unauthenticated here, or calling the tool would have side effects), say that explicitly to the user at publish time — in your reply, not as a note inside the published page — instead of shipping a guessed shape. Observed response payloads are the user's real data: learn the shape from them, but never embed the observed values in the published page as sample or placeholder data.

1	/**
2	 * The `mcp` capability — call the viewer's connected MCP tools from inside a frame.
3	 *
4	 * One decision, two arms: displaying data that should stay current is
5	 * `watchTool`; performing an action once is `callTool`. Use `listTools()`
6	 * to see which connectors the viewer has available. Calls run with the
7	 * viewer's credentials; your code never sees tokens. Obtain the
8	 * namespace with `const mcp = await claude.use("mcp")` — `null` means
9	 * this view cannot run the capability; design for absence.
10	 */
11	
12	declare namespace Claude {
13	  /**
14	   * Failure design — read before writing any call site. Connector calls
15	   * fail routinely in normal operation (lapsed auth, a connector the
16	   * viewer has not added, a briefly unreachable upstream), and each code
17	   * on {@link Claude.mcp.McpError} has a different correct response.
18	   * Design the page's degraded states alongside its happy path:
19	   *
20	   * - Branch the UX on the error `code`, never on message text, and
21	   *   never collapse all failures into one generic banner. A single
22	   *   catch-all ("transient connector failure", "something went wrong")
23	   *   is the named anti-pattern for this capability: it hides the one
24	   *   action that would fix the page (reconnect, add the connector,
25	   *   choose one, or simply wait) and turns recoverable states into
26	   *   dead ends. A default branch with generic copy is fine for codes
27	   *   you do not handle individually — the anti-pattern is collapsing
28	   *   the codes that do have a distinct fix into that one banner.
29	   * - Retry only errors stamped `retryable: true` (today
30	   *   `server_unavailable`, and `rate_limited` if it ever fires) — at
31	   *   most once per user-visible refresh, after a short randomized
32	   *   delay, honoring `retryAfterMs` when present, and ONLY for reads.
33	   *   `server_unavailable` (the runtime's reply timeout and upstream
34	   *   5xx land here) and `upstream_error` are AMBIGUOUS outcomes for
35	   *   writes: a rejection is NOT proof the tool did not run. Re-issue a
36	   *   write only behind a fresh user gesture, and where the connector
37	   *   offers a read, re-read state first. Never retry `needs_reauth` or
38	   *   `server_not_connected` unattended — repeating the call cannot
39	   *   succeed on its own: `needs_reauth` means credential refresh was
40	   *   already exhausted upstream, and `server_not_connected` means no
41	   *   connector is configured at all (for a `host:` server: no host
42	   *   bridge on this surface, or the local server is not running). Render
43	   *   their documented reconnect/add or no-host fallback copy instead; a
44	   *   later viewer action may bring a host server back.
45	   * - Consent is readable and requestable per connector via the
46	   *   `permissions` capability's scoped names: `"mcp:<server>"`, with
47	   *   the server name exactly as declared in the manifest (the same
48	   *   string passed to {@link Claude.mcp.callTool}). A multi-connector
49	   *   page should gate each section on its own server's state
50	   *   (`state("mcp:<server>")`) and ask per section
51	   *   (`request(["mcp:<server>"])`) rather than asking for everything
52	   *   up front; bare `"mcp"` remains the whole-manifest aggregate —
53	   *   "granted" only when every declared server is covered, and asking
54	   *   it asks for all of them. `use("mcp")` resolving non-`null` is
55	   *   the availability gate. Any state other
56	   *   than `"unavailable"` from a permissions read means present, and
57	   *   `"prompt"` means proceed (the first call asks) — never gate
58	   *   rendering on `=== "granted"`, and tolerate rejection on any
59	   *   permissions read (`.catch(() => "unavailable")`). Handle the
60	   *   lifecycle rejection codes on every call — availability is
61	   *   per-view and can change across a re-boot.
62	   * - A tool-level failure REJECTS with `tool_error` (the connector was
63	   *   reachable and answered, but reported failure) — the full result
64	   *   envelope rides the rejection's `result` field for the rare
65	   *   inspector. An immediate retry with the same arguments rarely
66	   *   helps; surface the reported message in the affected section.
67	   * - Host servers (`host:<name>`): a manifest entry whose `server`
68	   *   starts with `host:` names an MCP server running on the VIEWER'S
69	   *   DEVICE, reached through the Claude app that shows the page (the
70	   *   desktop app first). `<name>` is the local server's name with
71	   *   anything outside `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` replaced by `_`. The API is the
72	   *   same — `callTool("host:filesystem", "read_file", {...})`, consent
73	   *   per server via `"mcp:host:filesystem"` — with three differences:
74	   *   outside the app (a browser tab, an embedded drawer) every call
75	   *   fails — `server_not_connected` once the shell routes `host:`
76	   *   calls to the app; the service itself never runs a `host:` tool —
77	   *   and there `listTools()` then omits the server, so always render a
78	   *   no-host fallback; the app may ask the viewer to confirm a call
79	   *   that is not annotated read-only, which can take a while or come
80	   *   back `cancelled`; and only the Artifact's owner can use host
81	   *   servers for now. Once the shell routes `host:` calls to the app,
82	   *   tool input goes to the device rather than the service, which then
83	   *   sees which tool ran, never its arguments.

85	   *   multi-section reports) contain each failure in the section it
86	   *   affects: one failed call annotates or greys out its own section
87	   *   while the rest render normally. Keep the previous successful
88	   *   data visible with a stale/last-updated indicator (drive it from
89	   *   the result's `cache.storedAt`, never `Date.now()`), and prefer
90	   *   {@link Claude.mcp.watchTool} for such sections — it replays,
91	   *   refreshes, and coalesces for you. When every section fails at
92	   *   once with the same code, treat it as a page-level condition:
93	   *   show one message with a reload affordance instead of repeating
94	   *   the same error in every section.
95	   * - In a {@link Claude.mcp.watchTool} handler: transient errors keep
96	   *   last-good data; authz denials (`needs_reauth`,
97	   *   `server_not_connected`, `blocked_by_policy`, `approval_required`)
98	   *   RETRACT rendered data; registration failures mean no live updates
99	   *   will ever arrive — full doctrine on {@link Claude.mcp.watchTool}.

120	       * `retryAfterMs`. Never loop.
